question: Lyme disease – an illness caused by a bacterium called Borrelia burgdorferi and spread by ticks – is constantly gaining ground in Europe. Though Lyme disease is recognised as a rare illness, many Member States are still beset by critical diagnostic and therapeutic shortcomings, major regional disparities and the absence of specialised centres of expertise.

This state of affairs could result in EU citizens being subject to substantive discrimination. In some European countries, including Italy, patients’ associations are also complaining about the lack of recognition for chronic forms of Lyme disease and inadequately trained medical staff. In the light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission take concrete steps to support Member States in improving their diagnostic and therapeutic capabilities as regards Lyme disease?
Will the Commission promote a European research, clinical coordination and funding programme that can ensure equal treatment and protection for all European patients affected by Lyme disease?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.2.2026) 1. The Commission designated an EU reference laboratory (EURL) for public health in the field of high risk, emerging and zoonotic bacterial pathogens1, including Lyme borreliosis, which started its activities in January 20252 and is financially supported by the EU4Health Programme.

The EURL has been tasked with supporting national reference laboratories by providing reference diagnostics and test protocols, reference materials, external quality assessments, scientific advice, technical assistance and training. These activities will support Member States in implementing accurate diagnostic methods for Lyme borreliosis. Treatment of the infection varies across Member States.

The organisation and delivery of health services and medical care is a national competence3. 2. The EU has contributed to advancing research on Lyme disease through the Horizon research and innovation framework programmes, as well as the POCTEFA cross-border cooperation programme4.

Funded projects focused on improving diagnostic accuracy and addressing limitations of testing methods for Lyme disease, contributing to the development of more effective diagnostic tools, as well as on increasing the understanding of the risk of diseases such as Lyme disease. These projects represent an estimated investment of approximately EUR 16.5 million.

In addition, the Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026 includes an opportunity for research proposals on vector-borne diseases such as Lyme disease5. Direct grants from the EU4Health Programme were allocated to Member States to carry out surveillance in animals and the environment for cross-border pathogens, with a budget of EUR 20 million and for implementation in 2024-20266.
